Childminder's note, Maria D'Costa, holiday afternoons, Wednesday.
Simran (9) arrived after lunch and announced, "I'm bored," four times in the first twenty minutes. She lay on the floor, then on the sofa, then under the table. I didn't offer the tablet or a craft; I told her she could help me fold clothes or find her own thing. She groaned.
At about quarter to three, she went quiet. I found her at the dining table with scrap paper, a stapler and my old newspaper. She had started "The Colony Times": a report on the new stray kitten, an interview with the watchman (she went down and asked him three questions), and a weather forecast: "Hot. Still hot."
When her mother came, Simran made her buy a copy for one rupee.
Plan: leave the scrap-paper box out on Friday.

Tuesday, at Nana's house

Diary, today was the BORINGEST day of the holidays. It rained all afternoon, the power went, and Nana was sleeping. No TV. No phone signal in the village. I said "I'm bored" to Nani so many times she started saying it back to me.
Kishore and I lay on the verandah looking at the rain for about a hundred years. Then I noticed the water running down the drain along the courtyard really fast. I tore a page from my old notebook and made a boat. Kishore made one too. We raced them from the tulsi pot to the gate. Then we made rules: a boat that sinks loses three points, a boat that gets stuck on a leaf can be poked once with a stick.
I won 14 to 11. Kishore says he wants a rematch tomorrow. I hope it rains.
Ujjwal

qa.a: Kishore probably feels a bit competitive but excited, which is why he wants a rematch tomorrow.

When I was nine, in our village near Nashik, summer afternoons were endless. No television, no phone. The adults slept, the dogs slept, even the crows seemed to sleep. I lay on the verandah floor and said, "I'm bored," to the ceiling, over and over. My mother just said, "Good," and went back to sleep.
I was so cross. For an hour I did nothing. Kicked the wall. Counted flies.
Then I found a pile of bottle caps near the well. I made them into an army, and the cracks in the floor became rivers. By evening I'd built a whole kingdom.
I'm Jeevan, and I played that game all summer, beta.

Sunday, 2nd day of Diwali holidays

BORED. Wrote that word in my head about fifty times today. Shreya is at her Nani's, the TV is 'resting' (Mummy's word), and it's too hot to go out even though it's October. I lay on the floor and looked at the fan. Went round and round. I said 'I'm bored' to Mummy three times. She said, 'Okay,' and kept chopping. So after lunch I sat under the dining table. Then I thought, what if this is a cave? I put a bedsheet over it. I brought a torch. I made a map of the cave with the unused Diwali cards. Then I made the diyas into cave treasure. I didn't notice the whole afternoon go. Mummy peeked in at six and said, 'Explorer, dinner.' Tomorrow the cave gets a door.

Parul
